analysis.one_liner: Taxes large oil companies' windfall profits and sends the money back to households as gasoline rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2023 with 18 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil sold above its 2015-2019 average price, applying only to companies that extract or import more than 300,000 barrels a day. All the money collected would go into a "Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund" and be paid back to individual taxpayers as a gasoline price rebate, phasing out for higher incomes. It never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, lower- and middle-income households would have received per-person gasoline rebates funded entirely by a tax on large oil producers and importers, with the payments phasing out for households above roughly $75,000 in income ($150,000 for couples).

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax of 50% of the amount by which Brent crude's quarterly average price exceeds its 2015-2019 average, on companies that extract or import more than 300,000 barrels a day.

Recycles the money collected into a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and pays it out as per-person gasoline price rebates on tax returns, fully refundable so households owing no income tax still receive it.
Phases the rebate down for higher incomes, so payments go to households under roughly $75,000 ($150,000 for couples).

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers and importers — companies extracting or importing over 300,000 barrels daily — would pay the excise tax on each barrel above the pre-pandemic price baseline.

drawbacks.text: A per-barrel tax on crude oil would raise producers' costs, and oil companies could pass part of it to consumers at the pump, which would blunt the rebate's benefit during exactly the high-price periods when it applies.

The tax applies to every barrel sold above a pre-2015 price baseline rather than to profits that are demonstrably 'windfall' from market manipulation, so it functions closer to an income-tax surcharge on oil producers than a narrow penalty for price gouging.
The rebate phases out above $75,000 of income ($150,000 for joint filers), so higher-earning working households get nothing even though they also pay high gas prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit would have been a transfer of a share of oil-industry windfall profits back to consumers through per-person rebates, weighted toward lower- and middle-income households. The main costs and risks: a per-barrel tax on oil could feed into gasoline prices, partially offsetting the rebate, and could modestly discourage domestic production; the 50% rate on the amount above the 2015-2019 price baseline is a blunt instrument that does not distinguish price increases caused by supply shocks from those caused by market power. On balance, the design is reasonable and targeted, but the bill never advanced far enough to face that test.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Ro Khanna introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on February 14, 2023.

The bill taxed large crude oil producers and importers at 50% of the amount by which oil prices exceeded their 2015-2019 average, and rebated the revenue to individual taxpayers through a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund.'
The only action ever taken was a same-day referral to the House Ways and Means Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without any committee or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies kept the windfall profits the bill would have taxed, and no rebates were paid; the Ways and Means leadership that never scheduled the bill faced no vote on it.

for.name: 18 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Nadler, Pocan, Schakowsky, and Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the referred bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill drew no Republican support and never reached a vote, so the outcome was decided by a Democratic-run committee declining to act on a Democratic bill's priorities.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: Companies extracting or importing over 300,000 barrels per day would pay a 50% excise tax on each barrel's price above a 2015-2019 baseline. Small producers are exempt. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against consumers who would have received the rebates.
